title: Zero-Downtime Deployments: Strategies, Flags and Migrations
summary: Quick revision notes on recreate, rolling, blue-green and canary deployments, feature flags, and database migrations during deploys. Covers the mental model, the workflow for each strategy, common mistakes, and a cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Deployment Strategy Mental Model
points: Deploy vs release: deploy puts code on servers, release exposes it to users. Feature flags and traffic shifting separate the two.
Zero-downtime needs three things: a health check that gates traffic, graceful shutdown (drain in-flight requests), and old and new versions that can run side by side.

Every strategy trades off cost, speed, rollback time and blast radius. Strategies in rough order of increasing safety (smaller blast radius): recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary. Blue-green costs the most (about 2x infrastructure); canary needs only a small extra slice.
Blast radius is the share of users hit by a bad release. Recreate affects 100%, rolling affects a growing share, canary affects a small slice (e.g. 1-5%), blue-green affects 0% until the switch.
Mistake: treating a green CI run as proof the release is safe. Rollout safety comes from health checks, metrics gates and a tested rollback path.

chapters.title: Recreate and Rolling Updates
points: Recreate: stop all old instances, then start the new ones. It causes downtime but never runs two versions at once, so it suits breaking schema changes and dev environments.

Rolling: replace instances in small batches. Tune batch size with Kubernetes maxSurge (extra pods allowed) and maxUnavailable (pods allowed down). maxUnavailable: 0 keeps full capacity during the rollout.
Rolling needs readiness probes, otherwise traffic reaches pods that are not ready. Add preStop sleep plus terminationGracePeriodSeconds to drain connections.
Commands: kubectl set image deploy/app app=img:v2, then kubectl rollout status deploy/app, kubectl rollout undo deploy/app, kubectl rollout history deploy/app.
Mistake: during a rolling update v1 and v2 serve traffic together. Incompatible APIs, schemas or cache formats break requests mid-rollout.

chapters.title: Blue-Green and Canary Releases
points: Blue-green: run two full environments. Deploy and test the idle one (green), then flip the router, load balancer or Service selector. Rollback is flipping back, with no redeploy.
Blue-green cost: roughly 2x infrastructure during the switch. The shared database must be compatible with both versions, because only the app tier is duplicated.

Canary: send a small share of traffic (1%, 5%, 25%, 100%) to the new version and compare error rate, latency p99 and business metrics against the baseline before each step. Abort and roll back automatically on a breach.
Tools: weighted routing (Istio VirtualService weights, ALB weighted target groups), Argo Rollouts and Flagger for automated analysis and promotion.
Mistake: canary with too little traffic or no automated metrics gate proves nothing. Sticky sessions and a stale blue environment kept running long after cutover are the other common traps.

chapters.title: Feature Flags and Dark Launches
points: Feature flag: a runtime conditional (if flags.isEnabled('new-checkout', user)) that decouples deploy from release. Turning the flag off is a rollback with no redeploy.
Flag types: release flags (short-lived), ops kill switches (long-lived), experiment flags (A/B), permission flags. Targeting options: percentage rollout, user segment, internal users first.
Dark launch: ship code to production and run it hidden, for example by shadowing real traffic. Compare results before any user sees them.
Flags and strategies stack: deploy by rolling update with the flag off, then ramp the flag 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%. Evaluate with a stable user hash so each user keeps a consistent experience.

Mistake: flag debt. Release flags left in the code create dead branches and untested combinations. Remove them after full rollout, and give every flag an owner and expiry date. Also set a safe default for when the flag service is unreachable.

chapters.title: Zero-Downtime Database Migrations
points: Core rule: every schema change must be backward compatible with the code currently running. Old and new app versions both hit the same database during any rollout.

Expand and contract: 1) expand by adding the new column or table (nullable or defaulted), 2) deploy code that writes both and still reads old, 3) backfill in batches, 4) switch reads, 5) contract by dropping the old column in a later release.
Rename a column safely: add the new column, dual-write, backfill, move reads, then drop the old one. A direct RENAME breaks old code instantly.
Avoid long locks: add indexes with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (Postgres), backfill in small batches, set lock_timeout, and use online tools such as gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change on MySQL.

Mistake: running a destructive migration (DROP COLUMN, NOT NULL without default, type change) in the same release as the code change. A rollback then has no schema to fall back on. Ship additive migrations separately and before the code that needs them; drop or narrow columns only in a later release, once no running code uses them.

chapters.title: Zero-Downtime Deploy Cheat Sheet
points: Strategy table: Recreate (downtime, 1x cost, rollback by redeploy), Rolling (no downtime, 1x+ cost, slow rollback), Blue-green (no downtime, 2x cost, instant rollback), Canary (no downtime, small extra cost, stop and shift weights back).
Rolling update checklist: readiness probe, maxUnavailable: 0, preStop drain, terminationGracePeriodSeconds, kubectl rollout status/undo.
Canary checklist: start at 1-5%, compare error rate and p99 against baseline, automate abort, then promote in steps.
Flag checklist: default off, percentage ramp, kill switch, owner and expiry, remove after rollout.
Migration checklist: expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract later. Use CONCURRENTLY, batches and lock_timeout; never ship destructive DDL with the code change.
